utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm aware that presumably today this witness, Mr. Begic, will for the first time mark an exhibit, and sometimes there is a need that marking is done not only on the request of the Prosecution but sometimes the Defence wants some additional marking. Let's try to have one plain rule: Marking for the Prosecution is done in blue, and marking for the Defence is done in black, so that later on we're always able to identify whether the specific marking was made on the request of the Prosecution or of the Defence. If there is no preliminary issue, I'd like to ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Begic into the courtroom. And for the record, as far as the appearances are concerned, we see that Mrs. Annink has taken over again from her colleague of yesterday, and Mr. Stewart is still absent. Mr. Resch and Mr. Hannis being present for the Prosecution, and Ms. Loukas for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Begic. Please be seated. May I remind you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Yes. Mr. Resch, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, you had told us about the events, the beginning of the events on the 31st of May, and some soldiers escorting you and some of your family members from Donji Begici up to Gornji Begici; is that about correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For Your Honours' information, the events of 31 May are referred to in Schedule A to the indictment, incident 14.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers were there in Gornji Begici when all of the -- all of the Muslim citizens were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say how many there were exactly, how many soldiers in all throughout the village, because the whole village was somehow under an occupation. You could see soldiers everywhere; around every corner, around every hedge, behind the houses, so I really can't give you an approximation or the exact number at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That's fine. What did the soldiers ask you to do, you and the other men and women and children?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When our group from the direction of Donji Begici arrived in Gornji Begici, at that point in time the inhabitants of Gornji Begici who were in their basements -- in the basement or cellar of Safet Begic's house were ordered to step outside and line up on that little square in the little hamlet, and that's what they did. They went outside. We were in the process of arriving, and we were ordered or, rather, the order came that the men should line up on the left-hand side of the road and the women and children should go into Ismet Kurbegovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did these soldiers tell you or -- tell you what you were to do after you'd lined up on this left side of the road?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said we should make a column, stand in line one by one, turn towards -- our faces turned towards them. So we stood up against a house, and we were left alone. The women and children had already left that area, the area where we were standing. So we were left there on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did these soldiers tell you where you were going?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers told us that that group would go towards the Vrposki [as interpreted] bridge where buses would be waiting to transport us to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: The transcript says "Vrposki bridge." Do you mean Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vrhpolje bridge. There was just one Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you walk or were you put into buses or trucks? How did you -- how did you start out?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that place, we went towards the Vrhpolje bridge two by two, in a column two by two, not taking the road leading to the bridge but going across the vineyards, which is the area between Begici and Hrustovi. It's a hilly area. We went through some orchards in order to arrive at the Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: If Exhibit P117 could be put on the ELMO for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, if you could just take a blue pen, and on that map just draw the route, to the best of your recollection, where the -- your group started on the 31st of May and the route that you took to Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has indicated a blue line starting in Begici, heading initially south, thereafter south-east and then turning eventually back up to the north, ending at Vrhpolje bridge. Do you remember approximately how many soldiers were escorting the group of men from Begici towards Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were escorted by eight soldiers, eight armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you know the names of any of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew Jadranko Palija. He was the leader of that group escorting us, whereas I didn't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were there with you? How many prisoners, I think it's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were you all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the other 19 men, approximately, who were with you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Ceric Miralem, with two sons, Ceric Enes and Ceric Midhet. Then there was Hakija Begic with his son Muharem Begic, and then there was an elderly man called Sacir Begic. And with us also there was Safet Begic, Muhamed Begic with his son Fuad Begic, and his grandson Elmedin Begic. Then there was Nail Begic. Ismet Kurbegovic was another one, Munib Begic, Nedzad Begic, myself, Ismet Dizdarevic with three sons, Muhamed Dizdarevic, Mirsad Dizdarevic, and Enes Dizdarevic. I think I've given you all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That may not add up to 20, but is it possible there were some other men who were there that you don't remember their names?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean up on the bridge or escorting us?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me be clear. Other prisoners. You don't necessarily remember all the names of all the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do remember them all, but I don't know if I've missed any. If I've given you 20 names, then that's it, but I said about 20, but I know them all, and I think that I have stated who they were, but I might have missed some, although I do know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That's fine. Along the way to the bridge, did anything -- did anything happen that you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Walking towards the bridge or, rather, going towards the bridge, setting out from the village of Begici, we were first stopped by a weekend cottage which was in an orchard near Begici, and a group of Serb soldiers were resting up there, and they stopped us. They provoked us, swore at us. But truth to tell, they didn't abuse us physically at all. So after stopping there a while, we set off again in the direction of the bridge. And let me just add that some of the prisoners on that day had terrible consequences from -- that is to say they had been physically beaten up. When they were -- Kurbegovic Ismet, Begic Sacir, when the Serb soldiers entered the village in the first place, and our neighbours beat them up twice while they were entering the village, so that -- and they were suffering from the beatings. So we had Mr. Begic Sacir, who was walking along with us, and we had to drag him along, in fact, because we were told that if he lagged behind, he would be killed. They would kill him. Once we arrived in Hrustovacka Stanica, the first hamlet, across the bridge across the river Sanica, while we were crossing the bridge, Miralem Ceric, who had some heart problems, seemed to have a heart -- be having a heart attack. He had problems with his heart at that point, and his son Enes Ceric, who was helping him to walk along, lagged behind the column a little bit. And Jadranko Palija, at that point, took the two of them out and, right by the bridge across the river Sanica, took them to the former abattoir, the slaughterhouse, which was used by the butcher, and all trace is lost of them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you hear any shots from this butcher shop?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our column didn't lag behind. When I heard one shot, I turned round and several seconds later I saw Jadranko coming out of the slaughterhouse, placing his pistol back in its halter and joining up with the column again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: If you could take a look at Exhibit P117 on the ELMO. Do you see a photograph of the butcher shop?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's photograph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately along that map where that butcher shop was located, along the route that you drew? If you could take the pen and draw, I think it would be appropriate, a number 3 to identify where you remember the butcher shop.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, it is located right by the bridge across the river Sanica. That would be here, right up against the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has indicated a number 3 at the location where the route turns immediately to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: As this -- as your group continued along, was anyone else shot before you reached the Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After coming up onto the road again leading from Sanski Most to Kljuc, there's a crossroads, and on that crossroads Jadranko Palija took Ismet Kurbegovic out, and I mentioned the man a moment ago. As far as I know, he accused him of being in possession of a sniper, and allegedly that's why they had beaten him up. So at that point in time when Jadranko took him out at that crossroads, he pointed a pistol at him and asked him where his sniper was. Ismet said he didn't have any sniper, and then he killed him in cold blood, right up on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did Jadranko Palija kill anyone else on the way to Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After killing Ismet Kurbegovic, we continued along our journey. We didn't stop at all. We continued going towards the bridge, and 50 metres from the bridge, before we reached the bridge -- we were walking on the left-hand side towards the bridge. Behind us at that point, a small army van turned up with just one driver in it, and when he passed by the column, Jadranko stopped him and got in next to the driver. The window was open on the driver's side, and Jadranko ordered Irfan Begic to come to the other side of the van. Irfan went to the other side of the van and, without a single word uttered, this one who was sitting in the van shot at him with a pistol. And Irfan's body fell to the ground in a puddle by the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: How far away were you when Jadranko Palija shot Irfan Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the width or breadth of the road; two and a half to three metres, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next -- the photograph which has not yet been marked. Could this be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P118.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you recognise the photograph, the bridge in the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: On this photograph, can you see the location where Jadranko Palija shot Ismet Kurbegovic on the 31st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that. If you look here, you'll see a crossroads, so we were coming from the Hrustovo direction and moving on the left-hand side, and at this place, the very crossroads but on the other side, there was a Stop sign. So it was right up at the Stop sign where Ismet Kurbegovic was shot and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: To the best of your ability, could you just put a number 1 and circle it where you recall Ismet Kurbegovic was when he was shot.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Can you see on this photograph where Jadranko Palija shot Irfan Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it much better here. So as I said, approximately 50 metres before the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could you put a number 2 where Jadranko Palija shot Irfan Begic.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: When you arrived at Vrhpolje bridge, were there any other soldiers, any additional soldiers there waiting?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were many soldiers there at the bridge itself. To the left of the bridge there was a group of soldiers waiting, and at the crossroads where the road forks off to Kozica and Sanski Most, just by the bridge, a bit further down, there was a bunker, and you could see other soldiers there inside the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers were waiting at the bridge when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I didn't count them. If you count those inside the bunker and those standing around it, I think about 50 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did these soldiers have weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they all had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these soldiers that were waiting at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I recognised some soldiers like Marinko Acimovic, Predrag Stojnovic, Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did any soldiers -- any of these soldiers that were waiting at the bridge say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They kept taunting us after we'd arrived, and as we were walking on the left-hand side towards the bridge, they told us to cross to the other side of the bridge and to line up one-by-one by the fence along the length of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could you put a number 3 at the location where you were ordered to line up.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has indicated a 3 approximately mid-span of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: The soldiers that you found when you arrived at the bridge, you gave us some of their names. Do you know their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs. Among them there was also Nenad Kaurim, another man, Vidovic, and an ambulance driver who was not wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did you know Nenad Kaurim from before?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew all of them from before, all those lads. Some of them were my schoolmates. Some of them we used to play sports together. We were neighbours. I knew them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did Nenad Kaurim say anything to you at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nenad told us to line up along the side of the bridge, to take our clothes off and our shoes so they could search us. He swore at us. He kept saying bad things about us. And he said that on that day, they would kill 70 Muslims because seven Serb soldiers had been killed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: At the bridge did you or any of the other Muslim prisoners attempt to attack the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Begic, could you tell us what happened at the bridge. What did the soldiers do to you and the other Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They searched us quickly. They took away everything that we had. We threw our clothes in front of us down on the bridge, down the middle of the bridge, and then they asked whether there was anyone among us who could jump nicely into the river, and none of us said anything. And then Marinko Acimovic pointed at Midhet Ceric, who was the first in line looking from left to right. He said that Cera was very good at jumping into the water, and he ordered him to jump. Cera turned round, he climbed the fence, and jumped off. You could hear him swimming underneath the bridge as he was passing by. Marinko Kaurim and Zeljko were standing on the other side of the bridge, and they pointed their automatic rifles at him. When he appeared a little further down the stream, they fired a barrage of bullets at him and you could see his dead body floating down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did the Serb soldiers force anyone else to jump off the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After killing Cera, they said, "Come on, the next one." And it was Munib Begic's turn next. Munib Begic tried to explain something to them, to talk to them. However, they'd have none of that, and they cracked him over the head with a bat. So having been hit several times, he decided to jump, and he jumped the same way, and he swam underneath the bridge, and the same three or four soldiers fired at him. So his dead body, too, could be seen floating down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Looking again at the photograph Exhibit P118, what direction does the river flow?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The river flows this way. So from Kljuc on towards Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could you just draw an arrow on the map in the direction that the river flows.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has drawn an arrow indicating that the river flows from the left to the right as shown on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: From where you were standing on the bridge, could you see the men after they'd jumped into the water and passed underneath the bridge to the other side?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't really understand the question. If you jump into the water, you can see that, because these people were standing next to me. When they were passing underneath the bridge, you can't actually see them until you can see the other side of the bridge. That's ten or 15 metres down the river, and that's when you can see the body passing underneath the bridge, but not before that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Approximately how far is it from the surface the bridge to the surface of the water?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, six or seven metres, the drop. Perhaps more. About six or seven metres. Up to ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: The soldiers that were shooting at the prisoners after they jumped off the bridge, were they standing on the opposite side of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, they were standing on the other side of the bridge, looking down the river to the right of the bridge. That would be this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could you just draw a number 4 approximately where the soldiers who were shooting were standing.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has indicated a number 4 on the right-hand side of the bridge on the downstream side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did the soldiers continue to order prisoners to jump off the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Munib Begic had been killed, the next one was Mirsad Dizdarevic, one of the three sons of Ismet Dizdarevic who was also there. He was ordered to jump. This time they didn't beat him. He jumped. They fired at him. The same thing as with the two that came before. After him, it was the turn of their youngest brother, Enes Dizdarevic, who had turned 15 on that very day or was about 15 years of age, give or take a month or two. He was also ordered to jump. Without thinking twice, he crossed the fence, and at that moment Jadranko Palija walked up to him, raised a gun to his left temple and from a distance of about one metre shot him. His body was left hanging from the fence. And then Jadranko pushed the body with his leg from the fence and the body dropped into the river. Meanwhile, the soldiers kept firing away at the already dead body. After that, next to Enes there was Elvedin Begic. They wanted to question him. Briefly, they asked him who the commander had been at the village of Begici. Elvedin said he didn't know, that there was no one. At that point in time, one of the men hit him, and then the other soldiers came up and started beating us, all of them. It was from that moment on that they started beating the prisoners, all those who were at the bridge, including myself and everyone else. People were bleeding, and they would take them off the fence, back to the middle of the bridge, and there they would kick then and beat them. There was a house there, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was chaos there, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the man who was questioning Elvedin asked him whether there were any weapons back in the village and he said he didn't know, there had been no weapons. He said, as far as I can remember, I had a rifle, and then all of them, including Kaurim, started beating me. Jadranko walked up to me and told me to open my mouth, and he placed the barrel of an automatic rifle into my mouth and he was about to start firing, but Jadranko [sic] told him not to kill me on the bridge but, rather, to order me to jump down. So Jadranko said, "Okay, jump." I climbed over the fence just like everyone else, and I jumped off the bridge into the river, down the stream. I hit my head after I'd jumped because I plunged headlong into the river, so I hit a stone that was in the river with my head. I paused for a while just underneath the bridge. There was water all around, and you could still hear moans coming from those who were still on the bridge and were being beaten. I halted, and in a way took leave from my life. I took off the white shirt that I still had on. I pushed it down beneath the surface. I reckoned they would probably shoot me anyway, but I decided not to swim but, rather, to try to dive and reach the left river bank. And if I could manage that and dive down through the branches in the water, maybe I had a chance of staying alive, and in the end I succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You eventually reached the bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I dived through the bullets. They were still firing, I must say, but I kept looking at the white shirt that I had left behind, and the water carried it off in front of me, and I could see them firing, and the bullets were flying by my body. Fortunately, I was not hit. I managed to dive as far as the left river bank - you can see the couple of trees that were on the opposite river bank - and I surfaced again in the shrubbery that was just over the water, and I stayed there, holding onto the branches so they couldn't see me. From there I could see the bridge. However, I couldn't tell by the faces of the people falling into the water who they were. I was looking through the branches, and it was at some distance. My temple was bleeding. There was blood coming into my eyes. Therefore, I could not discern clearly who the next men were to jump. I reckoned there were about three or four other people who were made to jump, just like the ones before, and I didn't know what happened to the rest of them. I did find out later. You could hear a long burst of fire. After the beating, after the killings, you could hear a rather long burst of fire. I believe that that was when they were killed. There was silence after that and you heard nothing more, no one moaning, no one being thrown into the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Of all the men, all the prisoners who you named who were at the bridge that day, do you know if any of them survived?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Have you seen any of them alive after that day?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Over the following days, I was staying near the mouth of the river, near Sanica, because I was, myself, facing a difficult situation. I was trying to search that portion of the river, hoping that I would find survivors who could perhaps help me, but I found no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: One of the men you mentioned who was at the bridge was Nedzad Begic.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my younger brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Have you seen your younger brother since that day?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You eventually made it to a Serb neighbour's of yours, I believe, to his house?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You don't want me to talk about the other developments during those days, you just want me to talk about how I met my neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I think we can move ahead to meeting with your neighbour, and I think you were eventually taken to the medical centre in Tomina?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent several days at the mouth of the Sanica River, and that's where I came to. It was one of the nights, I think it was Thursday evening, there was a storm, and I decided to try to go to Vid Krlic's [phoen] house. We had been on friendly terms with those people, and we were even godfathers to each other's children, and I hoped that they could help me or perhaps provide some information or some medical assistance. I took advantage of the stormy weather and approached their house that night. The next morning, I announced my presence to them. I didn't come knocking at the door during the night, but rather, I came out of the stable and announced my presence to their sons who came out the next morning. They took me into the house, and Zeljko told me that there were no more survivors, that all of them had been killed at the bridge. His mother was also there inside the house, Andja Krlic, and Svetko from the town, who was a relation of theirs. I'm not sure what the reason was for his presence at the house. I told them what had happened. Andja Krlic said that Jadranko Palija, on his way back that day, first came to see them and said that he had tried to save their neighbours, the Begics, but he couldn't, he said, because the other people were attacking the bridge and that's why everyone was killed. At that moment my reaction was a bit brusque. I think I swore at them, saying that that was not true because Jadranko Palija personally killed the people there and that there was no fighting going on. I told them that the bridge never came under attack but that, rather, that was a deliberate killing. I talked to them briefly, and I asked to be given some clothes to wear. They brought some alcohol which I used to clean my wounds. I dressed the wounds on my head and my chest, and then I nodded off for a while. A little later, I heard voices. Neighbours had arrived and surrounded the house. I was ordered to come out. Once I was outside the house, standing there were the same people who had beaten their neighbours; Ismet Kurbegovic, Sacir Begic, Ranko Cosic, Ilic Vico, Bosko Stojkovic, and a colonel whom I had not known before. A lieutenant. The four of them arrived, and this lieutenant, who was their superior, asked them to tell them something about me. Andja Krlic and Zeljko Krlic told him that I could stay with them for a while, that they would nurse me back to health and keep an eye on me. However, three of the neighbours insisted that I be transferred immediately to Tomina, to the hospital there to undergo tests, allegedly. They tried to get a car to take me there, but I -- they couldn't find a car. And then after a brief consultation, they decided to take me there. So then we got into the car, and we went to Tomina. Near the elementary school there was a health station there, and Dr. Majkic was the physician who helped me. He cleaned the wound on my head. I told him about what had happened. I'm not sure why I did. And then they took me to the school where I was to be interrogated, allegedly, by Gojko Saula and Nedjo Sucur. When I came outside the school, I saw Gojko Saula leaving the school accompanied by Nedjo. He had received a phone call, an urgent call for him to come back to town. He turned to Nedjo and told him to interrogate me thoroughly and to leave me in the school building's cellar. Nedjo and myself went to the school building and into an empty room, classroom. We talked about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Can I stop you there for just a moment. This Nedjo Sucur, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedjo Sucur was a reserve officer of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you know what unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit of the 6th corps. In terms of rank, I'm not sure which rank he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Did Nedjo Sucur talk to you about the incident at Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about the whole thing. Nedjo recounted his own version of events in quite some detail, saying that whatever happened in that area was not supposed to happen and that he had nothing to do with the killings, that it wasn't his platoon that did it, that he felt awfully sorry about some of the people who were killed then. He told me about -- he asked me about how everything happened when we arrived at the bridge. He asked me if I remembered who fired at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he would have heard if it had been his soldiers, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what did you tell Nedjo Sucur about what happened at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I told Nedjo that we had arrived at the bridge, and while being in the process of arriving, the soldiers were beating us. As soon as we reached the bridge they started beating us and throwing us off the bridge into the water, therefore I was not able to see anything. It all happened very quickly, and I don't know who the soldiers were who were there. I couldn't -- I didn't even dare name those who I was sure were at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell him the names of the soldiers who were at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At that moment, I felt that it wouldn't have helped me and that it was better for me if I didn't say, didn't give the name of the soldiers, although after a brief conversation, he called Nenad Kaurim to the classroom and asked me whether I recognised the soldier, whether I knew him, and I said I knew that it was Nenad Kaurim, that I knew him from school, that I knew him from the checkpoint when he manned the checkpoint, because there were checkpoints that had been erected before that, several months prior to that, and that that's how I knew him. I said I don't remember him being on the bridge, so that he told Nenad he could leave after that brief encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You said it you felt it wouldn't have helped you to identify the soldiers. Did you feel intimidated or threatened during your questioning by Nedjo Sucur?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedjo Sucur didn't threaten me once during the interview. Not only that, but I had the feeling that I could trust the man, but the very fact of naming some of the soldiers I thought was not a good idea then and there, although I didn't think that any -- that I could expect mercy from any of them, but I didn't name the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: After your questioning, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that questioning, Nedjo went on to the second part, that is to discuss the events that took place in the area of Hrustovo Vrhpolje, and he told me that there had been some battles and fighting in Vrhpolje and that some people had been captured -- well, no, he didn't tell me about any capturing of the soldiers that stayed behind in Hrustovo. Some armed units, armed Muslim units, which I didn't know. And he also told me that he was shot at from Vrhpolje too. And he said that it was all a very ugly picture, all this that had gone on, that he was sorry, and that the inhabitants of Begici and Hrustovo, that they were in Tomina and that I would be escorted there as well. So he wanted to join me up with my mother and my youngest brother, who were in Tomina at the time, and he that I shouldn't tell anybody else about any of these events and that he would save me, and what he meant was that he would leave me in Tomina. And also he said that if ever I managed to leave Bosnia alive, that I should tell everybody that he saved my life. And I of course agreed to do that, and that's where our conversation ended. We got into his car, and they drove me off to Tomina, where my parents were or, rather, my mother, my brother, and some other refugees from the village of Hrustovo, in that house there, and that's where I was. I stayed there for about 20 days or one month in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Where were you -- where were you taken or where did you go after you left Tomina?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 4th of June when a couple of cars belonging to the Serb army turned up, and they had loudspeakers, and they ordered all the refugees from the neighbouring villages who were in Tomina at the time to come out of the houses, to line up by the Palma coffee bar, which is where the buses were parked to take them away. They said that nobody should attempt to hide, so that all the refugees from the surrounding villages came out onto the road where the buses were that day, and those were the buses they used to transport us to the camp of Krings, which was in Sanski Most, towards Uzlovci. And that was in the morning, at around 10.00 a.m., on the 4th of June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: How long were you held at Krings camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Krings -- well, I think it was the next day when they rounded up the women and children and some elderly persons. They gathered them together and took them off in an unknown direction. We stayed in the Krings camp for another two days, I think, and then after those two or three days, we were transferred by trucks to Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: When you were at Krings camp, were you free to leave?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Krings, they made a list of the people who stayed behind, but I didn't see them beat anyone. In the evening, someone might come into a room and mistreat them and threaten them with a knife, but there were no incidents, actually, nothing actually happened. There was no beating or -- there were no beatings or killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Who -- who was guarding the prisoners at Krings?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Krings there were the Serb soldiers again, the reserve formation of the Serb army, and they would take turns, replace each other. It was not always the same soldiers. Other guards turned up the next day, for example, whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You said you were transported by truck to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were other --

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trailer trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Were other prisoners transported in other trucks to Manjaca at the same time that you were?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day we were supposed to go to Manjaca, Krings turned up in the camp, or, rather, one or two trailer trucks belonging to the Agrokomerc firm, and there were some of the prisoners who were in Krings, and they were loaded up onto the trailer trucks, although I think several people stayed behind in the Krings camp. I don't know what happened to them afterwards. Perhaps they arrived later on or perhaps they were released, I don't know what happened to them. But once the truck was full, we were driven off to the sports hall which was in town, and we were told that we were going to wait for another truck that was being loaded up, that other people would be coming and taken to the sports hall or other camps around Sanski Most. We waited until the afternoon for these other trucks and for the convoy to be complete, and once all the trucks were full, we set off towards Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone died during this transfer in the trucks from Sanski Most to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the trucks to Manjaca, 20 prisoners succumbed, especially those who were beaten up in the camps in Sana, in the Betonara firm or in the MUP building. And I know that on the road to Manjaca they died, because when we arrived at Manjaca, when they called out our names when we stepped off the trucks and lined up, some of the people did not respond when their names were called out. And then the prison guards or camp guards would find the person lying dead in the truck. We heard them saying, "This one's dead." Then they would set them to one side, separate them. And according to what people said, I know that there were 20 such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: When you arrived at Manjaca, who was guarding that camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manjaca as a camp was unknown to us. We couldn't see who the soldiers were for a long time. We didn't see their faces for a long time because the inmates, when they arrived, the prisoners were ordered -- we were ordered to lower our heads and put our hands behind our backs. Our hands weren't tied behind our backs, but we had to clasp our hands behind our backs, and we were on no account allowed to raise our heads, so that we prisoners were not able to see who was actually guarding us. We know that they were Serb soldiers, of course, and they introduced themselves as such, but it was only after some 20 days had gone by, perhaps a little longer, that we were able to see where we were and who the people around us were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For how long were you held at Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was held at Manjaca camp until the 16th of December, which -- when I was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Where did you go when you were released?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They disbanded the camp three times or, rather, there were three departures; on the 14th, the 16th, and the 18th. I was released on the 16th of December and taken to Karlovac, the town of Karlovac, and from there I went to -- continued my journey to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could I have the final exhibit, the exhumation report, given a number and the B/C/S shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P119.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document entitled "Record on the Investigation and Exhumation of Bodies of Bosniaks from Mass Graves by the Bridge in Vrhpolje, Sanski Most Municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, could you take a look at pages -- the final two pages, 19 and 20, in the original version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's pages 20 and 21 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: There are 15 names, starting with Hasib Kadric, ending with Fuad Begic. Do you recognise any of these names as the other prisoners who were killed on the 31st of May, 1992, at Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this list we see under number 3, Irfan Begic; number 4, Muhamed Dizdarevic; number 11, Ismet Dizdarevic; number 12, Mirsad Dizdarevic; Miralem Ceric, number 13; and Hakija Begic, number 14; and Fuad Begic, number 15. These are the people who were on -- with me that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Resch. I'm wondering whether it would be wise to start cross-examination right now where we would still have ten minutes to go or whether to have an early break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's probably better to have an early break so I can do it in one component, and also in the interim I can get the lectern from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Begic, we will first have a break, and after the break you will be examined by Ms. Loukas who is counsel for the Defence. We will adjourn until a quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, welcome again in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Begic, first I want to take you to some evidence that you gave in relation to checkpoints. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now -- and I think you indicated that the people at the checkpoints were in fact your Serb neighbours dressed in army uniforms. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of there being checkpoints set up by Muslims as well in your surrounding area generally?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, the other aspect was I think you gave evidence that -- in relation to a person Mijatovic. Do you recall giving that evidence when you were giving the evidence about checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you were asked, you know, if he was a member of any particular military unit, and your response was: "Well, I really can't say. I think it was all the 6th Krajina group throughout that territory. Now, whether that unit had a special name, I really can't say." So, Mr. Begic, it would be true to say that whether it was the 6th Krajina Brigade is just your opinion, and you really can't be certain about that. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it was my opinion, but as I said in my first statement, I was present at a meeting which was organised by Branko Basara, for example, in March 1992, and it was held in Tomina, and Branko Basara personally said that the 6th Krajina Brigade was in charge of that area. So I came to the conclusion that all the units there, working there and operating there, belonged to the 6th Krajina Brigade in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Begic. Now, I just want to remind you of an answer that you gave in your previous testimony, and that's at page 6385 of the transcript in the case of Mr. Brdjanin and the late General Talic. You were asked this question and I just want to remind you of it, okay: You said that there were certain soldiers at this checkpoint and you said that they belonged to the 6th brigade. How did you know that they belonged to the 6th Brigade?" Your answer was: "As I've already said, over the media one could hear that the 6th Brigade was deployed in the area. No mention was made of any other units. At least, I don't know of any others. They wore the insignia on their clothing of the Serb army, and I believe that there was an indication that it was the 6th Krajina Brigade, but I'm not sure of that." Now, you, of course, recall giving evidence in that particular case, Mr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course what you said on that occasion was the truth?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So the -- the answer that you gave there, "I believe that there was indication that that was the 6th Krajina Brigade, but I'm not sure of that," that's the truth?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I personally heard from Colonel Branko Basara that in the area was the 6th Krajina Brigade, and I myself was distributed in the reserve force of the 6th Krajina Brigade which was operating in Sanski Most as a member of the TO. And through the media, on the radio, all we heard about was the 6th Krajina Brigade. No other units were ever mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Begic. Now, moving on to another area. You gave evidence in relation to the 25th of May, 1992, yesterday. Do you recall giving evidence in relation to that particular day?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I think that you gave evidence that on that day you went and hid from the soldiers. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that, those particular soldiers that came on the 25th of May, it would be true to say, would it not, that your identification of them is based on conversations that you had with your mother. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now -- oh, just in relation to this area of the -- of the men at the checkpoints, I just want to remind you of another answer you gave. "Would you allow for the possibility that these men that you saw --" sorry, this is page 6385, for the Court. The question is: "Would you allow for the possibility that these men that you saw that were wearing Serb symbols on their uniforms belonged to certain paramilitary units?" Do you remember being asked that question, Mr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And your response was: "I would not be able to say because I don't remember very well these symbols, so I'd rather not assert anything regarding the symbols and which unit they belonged to." Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course when you gave evidence on the last occasion, you were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And so it would be true to say, would it not, that -- that you don't remember very well the symbols and you'd rather not assert anything regarding the symbols and which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was that they were members of the 6th Krajina Brigade. Now, whether in the area or around about our villages there was any other smaller unit and whether it had a name of some kind, I wasn't aware of that, I didn't know about that, so I don't wish to testify. But I do know that at the checkpoint at Stojinici the commander was Ranko Cosic, the commander of those units. Now, what their unit's name was or what some of them were called, I never knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, do you allow for the possibility, Mr. Begic, that there were paramilitaries in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's even though you expressed this uncertainty in relation to this question on the last time you gave evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, despite that. Despite that testimony, I still claim that I was not aware of any other units, at least not that I was aware of any other unit with the exception of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Begic. Now, moving on to another area. Just in relation to the 31st of May, and you were asked this question: "Do you know what unit these soldiers were from?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could we have a page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's page 87 from the transcript yesterday, for the benefit of the Court and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So page 87 from the transcript yesterday, you were asked this question: "Do you know what unit these soldiers were from?" Do you recall that question in relation to the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, you don't recall the question. Okay. I'll give you the answer. That might prompt your memory. "No, I don't know which particular unit they belonged to, but I think they were all members of that unit which was located in a school in Klijevci." Do you recall that answer now?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recall that answer because my understanding of the question was which soldiers came to our village on that day, which unit they belonged to, knowing that on that day our neighbours had arrived in our village, and they belonged to Klijevci, and my understanding was that those would have been soldiers belonging to a unit that was part of the Klijevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that was your understanding; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that day again, the 31st of May, I'm just going to remind you of an answer you gave in the Brdjanin and Talic trial and ask you to confirm that. Do you understand where we're going now?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the 31st of May, you were asked this question at page 6389: "All the soldiers that arrived in your village that day, were they wearing the same uniforms?" And your response was: "The day they rounded us up on the 31st, there were different ones. There were those in SMB, the normal colour of uniforms, and camouflage uniforms, military camouflage uniforms. Some were wearing a helmet that day, and others had different hats on their heads. So I didn't look closely at their insignia." So do you recall that question and answer from your previous evidence, Mr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that you of course told the truth on that prior occasion?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to arriving at the bridge, I might remind you of another answer you gave on the previous occasion, and that is that -- again, that's on the 31st of May, when you arrived at the bridge. And you were asked this question, and I might give you a previous answer just to give you the context properly. Answer: "As we arrived at the bridge, one could notice a bunker at the crossroads towards the villages of Ilija and Tomina, and in the bunker around it there were quite a few soldiers. We were taken over by five or six of them who were standing right next to the bridge." You were then asked this question: "These soldiers that you're talking about, were they regular soldiers?" And your answer was: "No." Do you recall that question and answer from the previous trial?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course when you gave that evidence you were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And so these soldiers, as far as you could see, were not regular soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one final question, Mr. Begic. You also gave evidence today at page -- page 22 and page 23 of the transcript today in relation to who was guarding you at Krings. Do you recall giving questions in relation to that area of your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you indicated that that was the reserve formation of the Serb army. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course the basis of your assertion about that is, I suppose, that they were Serbs and wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but one thing I would like to add is their age. They didn't seem to be regular soldiers of a regular army. Someone aged about 50 could not have been a regular soldier belonging to a regular army unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours. I might indicate, Your Honour, that I will be tendering the previous evidence given in cross-examination by the witness so that the answers that have been given from the context of the previous trial will be available to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that you, I would say, used limited portions of that testimony. I have got no idea how many pages we would receive if you were to tender the whole of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was a relatively short cross-examination, so we're actually dealing with a very tiny amount. I can indicate, Your Honour, that it's -- yes, it's here, Your Honour. That's the nature of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Resch, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: No questions on re-examine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: With respect to the additional -- the submission of the previous cross-examination, I believe it's the Prosecution position that we would like seven days to review those materials and put in any materials from the direct examination that would put the cross-examination in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would introduce new evidence on which the Defence would then have had no possibility of asking additional questions. It's relatively short. How many pages were there?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps under these circumstances, Ms. Loukas, I think you referred to a couple of pages, for example, 6385, 6389, so a very limited number. I would say even if you take the context into account, it might not be more than five or six pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It's very limited. In fact, I don't need to tender the entire cross-examination. I can streamline it and limit it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that would be possible. And perhaps you could, in the copy you give to the Prosecution, you perhaps immediately now indicate what pages you use, so make that selection right away so that you can look at it, Mr. Resch, on the spot, and then I think there would be no further need to check on whether there's anything else because it's just the parts read by Ms. Loukas, and then of course you can see what the previous ten lines and following ten lines, but it's so limited that I'd rather not take any risk by introducing other parts of the examination in chief that we would have to recall the witness, so rather deal with it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case with these limited numbers, that's probably okay, but if this is a -- effectively a Rule 92 bis submission, the Rules do allow certain time limits for response and such, but again, if the pages are such that we have no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One could even consider, Ms. Loukas, you have read all the relevant portions you wanted to draw the attention to, so you could even reconsider whether 92 bis (D) would be necessary at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm just thinking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm having problems with this microphone. Your Honour, I would indicate that I will actually give it some thought. There may not even be a need to tender that material at all, quite frankly. The relevant matters I wanted to deal with, I dealt with with the witness. In fact, what that -- what I could do is just -- there's just one further question I'd need to ask, and we could leave it at that, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that would save paper, that would save all kind of complications that would cause us to ask the witness to come back, which is not something --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Which of course we want to avoid, Your Honour. So I think having covered those matters and highlighted the relevant portions of the previous cross-examination, there is no need for me to add to the Trial Chamber's bundle of papers. There is just one more question I would need to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas. Then put the one question you still have in mind to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be two, Your Honour, but it's one small area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Begic, I just want to ask you about the statement you gave to the Bosnian authorities some time ago. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before some time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In fact, I'm referring to when you were present with Mr. Adil Draganovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So that's the first statement that I gave to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Mr. Begic, yes. Now, who was -- who was in fact writing down what you were saying during that record of interview? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Adil Draganovic was there and Mr. Zijad -- I can't remember his last name. Zijad --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's okay, Mr. Begic. The name of the other person doesn't matter. All I wanted to know is who was actually writing down what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zijad.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you, Mr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to clear up two points if I may. The first is -- or, rather, the first concerns the incident that took place on the 31st of May at the point in time when you were crossing the bridge. You said, or, rather, that's how I understood it, that a certain Muharem Ceric and his son were taken, and a certain man called Jadranko, and you heard later on a shot, and you saw Jadranko with a pistol which he was putting back into its halter. If I understand correctly, there were two people, Ceric Muharem and his son, but you heard just one shot and you didn't speak about the other person, the son. Did the son came back? Did he disappear?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Miralem Ceric, if I can put you right there. He was an elderly man, and this event happened on the Sanica River, crossing the bridge, on photograph number 3. And I've already said that Miralem Ceric was -- had a heart condition, and after walking for some time across the hill, he had some heart problems, and his son Enes Ceric helped him along, helped him walk in the column. As they lagged behind the column several metres, Jadranko at that point took the two men out of the column and took them into the slaughterhouse where the cattle were slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's just what I said. But later on, you said that you heard one single shot, and Jadranko came back, but you didn't speak of the son. What happened to the son, Miralem Ceric? What happened to the son?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and the statement I gave two years ago, I said on the opposite side of the river. So we passed by the hamlet of Hrustovacka Stanica where there were some ten houses, maybe more, and we crossed the bridge. At that point in time when we were crossing the bridge, all the houses were on fire. They were burning. And there were a lot of soldiers among those houses who were shooting up in the air. Many cars were coming back. There was general chaos. And when I said that I heard just one shot at that point in time, the roof tiles were shattered, you could hear shots from other weapons. So I didn't say I heard two shots fired from a pistol. I heard one bullet fired, and I stand by that, one bullet fired by him. Now, whether he shot again, shot a second time, I can't say. But it is true that after that shot that I had heard coming from nearby, I did see him come out from where he was and place his pistol back into the halter and continue along with the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you're confirming that Miralem, the father, as well as his son, were taken out, taken off by Jadranko; is that right? And that you heard one single gunshot, but you didn't see the two people again; is that right? That is to say Miralem Ceric and his son.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is correct. The three of them went into the slaughterhouse, you could hear a shot, and you just saw Jadranko coming out himself and joining the column. We didn't see the other two men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the names of the people whose bodies were identified? And I'm going to read them out in English. [In English] Investigation of bodies of Bosniaks from mass graves by bridge. [Interpretation] And you identified, I believe, Miralem Ceric, but do you remember that you ever saw the name of his son? Did you see his son's name?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see his son's name there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you. Now, another question, please. If I understood you correctly, you said that on the 31st, after the incident that took place on the bridge, you went to Tomina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you also said that you stayed there for 20 days; right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but later on you said that on the 4th of June, vehicles turned up, armed vehicles, armoured vehicles, and they came to fetch you and transport you to Krings. So there seems to be a problem there. That is to say the principal incident that took place on the bridge took place on the 31st of May, and then you went on to say that you stayed in Tomina approximately 20 days, and then on the 4th of June you say that they came to fetch you. So there's a problem of time there.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five days went by from the 31st. That was a Sunday. On Friday, I was transferred to Tomina. So that was the 5th or the 4th. And then on the 4th of June, that's a little more than 20 days. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't understand. If you say that the 31st of May was the date of the incident on the bridge, and you went to Tomina, you stayed there for 20 days, where does that leave us? And on the 6th of June, you were taken to the camp, Krings camp.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But how could you have stayed in Tomina for 20 days? That's impossible, looking at the mathematics of it.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I didn't pay attention to -- of looking at the dates, from one date to the other, to give you the exact number of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour. It is more days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Begic, since I have no further questions for you, this concludes your -- yes, is there any question that arises from the questions by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Always the microphone. Yes. I'm not sure Your Honours have any further questions. I thought Your Honour was about to wrap up at this point, so there was just one point I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that is this: I just wondered if I could ask one further question on cross-examination, with your leave, because there was a question I neglected to ask on that last topic I was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may do so, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, just in relation to when you were giving that Bosnian statement, you mentioned that the other person was writing it down. I can't remember their name for the moment. Their name was Zijad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Zijad.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Zijad, yes. Now, they were writing it down. Who was dictating?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and Mr. Draganovic together. They took my statement and based their report on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. And I think it's the case, is it not, that at one stage -- well, I'll just give you this question from your previous cross-examination, just to remind you about it, okay? Just to put you in context. And it's this: "Question: In your written statement of the 16th of April, you said, 'I was taken to the SDS headquarters near the school --'"

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry. 6391.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "I was taken to the SDS headquarters near the school." "I should like to know whether you were taken to the school or to a house next to the school." And your response was: "No. They took me to the school, but I don't remember saying that it was the SDS headquarters." Do you recall that bit of your cross-examination, Mr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. And what I added was that inside that school, there was a unit, an army unit, that was stationed there. I knew some of the soldiers slept in the school building. I think their headquarters was actually at the school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Begic. Yes, I think that's the last question, Mr. Begic. I think I'll allow you to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Resch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did have a question following up on His Honour Judge El Mahdi's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Begic, although Ms. Loukas allowed you to go home, you have to stay for a second because there's another question for you. Please proceed, Mr. Resch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: With respect to the time line issue, the incident at Vrhpolje bridge was on the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: You were unconscious after that incident for a few days, so that takes us up to the 1st or 2nd or 3rd of June, approximately, when you went to your neighbour's house. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: From your neighbour's house you eventually went to the medical centre in Tomina?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: And from that point, from approximately the 3rd or 4th of June, it was another 20 days or so that you stayed in Tomina before you were then transported to Krings, so sometime late June, is it possible early July?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Okay. So it was probably early July when you went to Krings, not the 4th of June -- I'm sorry, to Manjaca. From Krings to Manjaca was sometime in early July?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I apologise for the small errors that I made in relation to the dates June, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That's okay. I think we've cleared that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Resch. Mr. Begic, you've answered all the questions. It's not the first time that you are in this Tribunal, so you are aware that questions come from both parties and from the Bench. You answered them all. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague, and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Begic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, Mr. Resch?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: The Prosecution is, Your Honour. Before we do that, I want to move into evidence the Exhibits P116 through P119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I think we could do that, at least, if Ms. Loukas has made up her mind meanwhile on the tendering of the transcript as an exhibit or whether we just leave it to the portions read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to leave it to the portions that have been read out, though I will make one point, Your Honour. An insistence on a seven-day 92 bis aspect in relation to should the Defence be wishing to tender a particular portion, I think is a little harsh, shall I put it that way, in view of the fact that in terms of equality of arms, we're dealing with eight different counsel on the Prosecution's side popping in and out and there's just two of us to deal with everything over here. So I think that that particular approach is, if I might say, a little severe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it is -- under 92 bis, it's -- I mean, that's what you call more or less an inequality doesn't change the Rule as such, but in the application of the Rule, of course, we could try to accommodate the parties. Mr. Resch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if in the future the Defence could advise the Prosecution in advance of the witness's testimony which pages they may want to offer, then that would allow us to take a look and see if there's any other cross or any additional previous testimony that may need to go in and we could probably deal with this ahead of time easier than we could at the end of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd like to make a comment, Your Honour. I've been listening to this. It is completely artificial, this problem proposed by the Prosecution, and frankly, when it comes to the overall weight of the case and the huge amounts of material that we're presented with, often very late, and the huge amounts of material that we have to digest, to suggest that this creates any significant problem at all for the Prosecution is entirely artificial, and to try to take advantage of the 92 bis procedures in this way to suggest that there is any serious problem we regard as -- well, I used the word artificial. It simply cannot be a problem by comparison with the position that the Defence face where we may not be able to take technical advantage of such matters as 92 bis but the reality is that we are constantly faced with vast amounts of material at the last minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
