utterances.text: Let me be clear. What is done here is that, for reasons of efficiency, the Defence has relied on very small portions of an earlier testimony and providing the -- the sources well in advance, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perhaps, Mr. Stewart, the Prosecution, which has provided under 92 bis sometimes more than a thousand pages, fears that, perhaps without reason, that the Defence might ever do the same and, therefore, reserve their position. I'm not saying that there's any justification for such fear at this moment, but one thing is true, that the Prosecution has provided huge amounts of transcript pages. So therefore, let's leave it at this very moment to the -- this case. We see that we have solved problem, and Mr. Resch has asked the attention for a proper opportunity to prepare, and I'm certain that he'll keep that in mind if he provides the Defence with lots of material so that the Defence will have a proper opportunity to prepare as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. I'm quite confident Mr. Resch will do that, and I'm quite confident we will deal with real problems when they really arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Let's not spend more time on it. Madam Registrar, could you guide us through the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P116, map of the ethnic composition of Sanski Most in 1991 and 1995. Exhibit P117, overview map of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje map, with names of villages and hamlets located around Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, with eight photos, and the map was marked by the witness. Exhibit P118, photograph of Vrhpolje bridge. Exhibit P119, Record on the Investigation and Exhumation of Bodies of Bosniaks from Mass Graves by the Bridge in Vrhpolje, Sanski Most. And P119.1, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, all these exhibits are admitted into evidence. I'd like to make one observation, Mr. Resch. At the beginning of the introduction of P Exhibit 117, I said something about the small pictures. I noticed, nevertheless, later, when the witness had testified about the butcher shop, you asked him whether he could find a butcher shop on this. Under 3, he said. Well, it reads next to number 3 that that's the butcher shop. I don't think that this would be a real contested issue, but I think it would have been better that if you want to put such a question to the witness that you leave out in your exhibit the indication that it's a butcher shop, and it would have served quite well to have it located in the area, or if you give eight pictures that he could choose, but he hardly could do anything else than choose number 3. At least, I would have done that. Apart from that, I do understand that the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness. There are no protective measures effective at this moment. Mr. Resch, is it you who is going to deal with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's Mr. Harmon. So if it's possible, I'd asked to be excused, and I believe Mr. Harmon will step in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Actually, it's myself and Ms. Annink being excused and a new team coming in for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could use the time while we're waiting for Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: An issue which has just been left for the moment we haven't dealt with because I think it does, in fairness, at least require Mr. Harmon to be in court and when neither he nor I have been here the last couple of days, is the question of the small clip of correspondence which we handed to the Trial Chamber, I think it was possibly even before the -- I forget before which adjournment, but it was some weeks ago anyway, correspondence between myself and Mr. Harmon and then between myself and Ms. Del Ponte, and at some point while Mr. Harmon and I are both in Court it would be convenient to deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have to bring this back into my mind exactly what position the Chamber takes in this respect and whether we have expressed anything about it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour hasn't. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, but I will stand corrected if we look at it again during the next break, the Chamber took notice of it and since there was no specific question of interfering specifically, the Chamber left it to that, but if the parties think that any position should be taken or that any position should be expressed, then we'll consider, first of all, whether we'll do that, and second, what -- if the first question has been answered in the positive, what that position would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I raised it now is because it seemed to me that after a little while it would be necessary for the Trial Chamber to have the opportunity of refreshing its mind on that correspondence. So I raised it so that the Trial Chamber would have the opportunity at some point, perhaps over a break because there isn't very much material, to do that, and then to raise the matter while Mr. Harmon is in Court. What I would wish to do is that, if the Trial Chamber could, and I would be extremely grateful if the Trial Chamber could at some point find some time to just quickly refresh yourselves as to the content of that material, then I would be able to raise the particular question which I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that, but I hope you will excuse us for not having the correspondence exactly in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I assumed that it wouldn't be at the top of Your Honour's mind at this moment, which is why I bring it up so that you do have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take that opportunity. Mr. Harmon, you are taking the next witness, which is a witness without any protective measures, and is Mr. Kirudja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you now please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the witness is escorted into the court, if I could have the lectern. We seem to have only one lectern for a busy courtroom and I would appreciate having the usher's assistance in having it brought to this side of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, may I invite you to stand. Before giving evidence in this court -- you followed my first words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text is now handed to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw, Mr. Kirudja, that you were unloading your bag and you have quite some documents in front of you. May I instruct you not to consult these documents unless given permission to do so, because you are -- of course, if you have to consult them, please tell us so it's clear whether you're consulting your memory or whether you're consulting any papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution, will examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I'm going to ask you some questions about your background, and the way I propose to proceed is I will identify some information and merely ask you to affirm the information is correct. So let me begin, Mr. Kirudja, with the following: You were born on the 20th of April, 1946. You are a citizen of Kenya. You hold a bachelor's degree with honours in applied economics from the University of Nairobi; an MBA from York University in Toronto, Canada; and a Ph.D. in management science from the University of Western Ontario, in Canada; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You joined the United Nations in 1977. During your United Nations service in the former Yugoslavia, you served as civil affairs coordinator in Sector North in Croatia from April of 1992 until March of 1994. From March of 1994 to August of 1994, you were assigned to the UNPROFOR United Nations Protective Force headquarters in Zagreb on civil affairs related issues; and from August of 1994 to June of 1995, you served as a delegate and special representative of the Secretary-General to the government of the Socialist Federal Republic -- I'm sorry, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If Mr. Kirudja could be shown the first exhibit, which is a copy of his statement. If I could have a number for that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P120.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you have a copy of Prosecutor's Exhibit 120 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I have a copy of a document that I recognise to be a statement from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that is a statement that was taken from you between the 13th and the 23rd of September, 1999, and on the 28th and the 29th of September, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And your signature appears at the end of that statement, and your initials appear on the pages of that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that a true and accurate copy of the statement that you signed and initialed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, Mr. Kirudja's original statement was considerably longer. It was 62 pages of text, and it had 277 numbered paragraphs. I have redacted paragraphs that were not relevant, and I have, therefore, submitted to Your Honours as Exhibit 120 the abbreviated redacted statement of Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the full statement was disclosed at an earlier stage to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I comment? Yes, indeed it was. I think this is just the appropriate point to mention this. It would have been helpful if we had known of the redactions sooner, because, with everything else that's to be done, although it wasn't difficult for me to see that the second half of this statement was less relevant than the first half, that was fairly obvious from an intelligent reading, nevertheless until about 48 hours ago, I was working on the footing and the assumption that Mr. Kirudja's statement which was going to be used for evidence was the 60-something page statement, and it would have saved time and it would have saved effort, given that both are at a premium, if I had known that rather earlier. It's not -- I don't say this is the biggest issue in the case because I was able to form, I hope, an intelligent assessment of the relative weight but I do make that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, there are is quite some time restraint on all parties, and if it is clear that only part of a statement will be used, I don't know exactly when you disclosed, I would say the abbreviated version of the statement to the Defence, but if this is done well in advance of the witness appearing in court, it certainly would facilitate the other party. I would expect the same from the Defence, but I think it's a fair comment made by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take Mr. Stewart's point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to tender this statement, Your Honour, pursuant to Rule 89(F). And now if I could, with the Court's indulgence, read a summary of the written evidence that is found in Exhibit 120. I have provided a copy of this summary to both the Trial Chamber and to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. I think we've -- yes. And you're going to read the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, is a summary of the written evidence. I proceed as follows: Mr. Kirudja is a United Nations employee who has been with the organisation since 1977 where he has held numerous important positions. From April 1992 till March 1994, Mr. Kirudja served as a civil affairs coordinator in one of the four United Nations protected areas, those were known as UNPAs, Sector North in Croatia. From March 1994 until August 1994, he continued to work on civil affairs related issues at UNPROFOR UNPF headquarters in Zagreb; and from August 1994 to June 1995, he served as delegate of the special representative of the Secretary-General to the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Mr. Kirudja, who is a citizen of Kenya, holds a bachelor's degree from the University of Kenya, a master's degree from York University, and a doctorate from the University of Western Ontario. Mr. Kirudja's statement describes the mandate of the UNPROFOR mission in Croatia and his role as civil affairs coordinator in Sector North. His responsibility was to ensure that the UN mandate in Sector North was implemented. He arrived in Sector North on 19 April 1992. Sector North occupied a part of Croatia that was on the border with Bosnia, the two countries separated by the Una River. The international border between those two countries in parts of Sector North was, for all intents and purposes, non-existent since Sector North was controlled by the Croatian Serbs and Bosanski Novi was controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. On 26 May 1992, Mr. Kirudja met with the mayor of Dvor, Jugoslav Borojevic, and others. Dvor is located in Sector North on the Croatian Bosnian border directly across the Una River from the municipality of Bosanski Novi. The mayor informed Mr. Kirudja that 5.000 Bosnian Muslims from Bosanski Novi would be travelling from Bosnia to Austria and Slovenia through Sector North and that he, the mayor, had agreed to this development on two conditions; that the passage be filmed by an international television crew to demonstrate that they had passed through Serb-controlled territory safely and that UNPROFOR and ICRC be responsible for them during transit. The mayor explained that he had spoken to the mayor of Bosanski Novi in Bosnia and confirmed that the Bosnian Muslims were leaving Bosanski Novi "voluntarily." Mr. Kirudja inquired why the mayor of Dvor was speaking on behalf of a mayor from a different town in a different country. Mr. Borojevic replied that Bosanski Novi was part of a "new reality" in the form of the "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Mr. Kirudja concluded that for all intents and purposes, the international border in this section of Sector North was non-existent. Mr. Borojevic endeavoured to convince Mr. Kirudja that the Muslims from Bosanski Novi wanted to leave and telephoned the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Pasic, but Mr. Kirudja declined to speak to him. After this meeting, Mr. Kirudja concluded that the mayors of Dvor and Bosanski Novi were acting in concert to engineer a massive evacuation under the guise of humanitarian assistance, beginning with some 5.000 Muslim residents of Bosanski Novi and to talk UNPROFOR into accepting responsibility for the transit of these people. On the following day, having failed to convince Mr. Kirudja to participate in this scheme, a delegation from Bosanski Novi arrived unannounced in Mr. Kirudja's office. This delegation included Radomir Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi; Rade Palija, a member of the Bosanski Novi municipal Executive Committee; and the Bosanski Novi chief of police. Mr. Pasic informed Mr. Kirudja that 5.000 of Bosanski Novi's 13.000 Muslims had asked the authorities for protection and had conveyed their wish to travel in a convoy to Austria and Germany. Mr. Kirudja inquired why Muslims wanted to leave their homes if everything was as peaceful as portrayed. Mayor Pasic responded, "I admit that the Muslims have been under pressure from armed Serbian irregulars," implying that the regular forces of law and order had nothing to do with the harassment of the Muslims. He informed Mr. Kirudja that two Muslim spokespersons from Bosanski Novi had been identified, a gentleman by the name of S. Bajraktarovic, a local SDS leader, and Fikret Hamzagic, an elected member of the Bosanski Novi municipal government. Mayor Pasic also informed Mr. Kirudja that the authorities of Bosanski Krajina had decided that all armed troops were to be disarmed and that the disarming process was carried out in the following manner: Between 6 and 8 May, meetings were held between the SDS and the SDA. An agreement was reached that all paramilitary groups were to be disarmed by 11 May. A schedule of disarmament, village by village, was discussed with a deadline of 9 May for the completion of this exercise. The SDA said that they still had arms so that no arms were collected from them. Mayor Pasic said that 5.000 people from certain villages had refused to disarm. Based on his conversations with the Bosnian Serb representatives, Mr. Kirudja concluded that the Muslims did not want to leave voluntarily and that they were being forced out of Bosanski Novi because they had first refused to sign allegiance to a newly created Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that this was later compounded by their refusal to relinquish whatever arms they had for self-defence. Mayor Pasic continued. He said that: "The Serbian police had been attacked and that the conflict began." He said that "The region had been under the authority of the Serb Republic of BiH since 10 May and that the legal authorities were thus forced to respond against Muslims since none of them had disarmed." I may have misquoted what is said. "Since some of them did not disarm." Mr. Kirudja asked members of the Serb delegation why Serbs -- why the Serbs and the Muslims could no longer live together as they had in the past. And mayor Pasic replied, "The former police officers who were Muslims refused to sign loyalty oaths to the new government." Mayor Pasic went on to explain that the Muslims were not true pacifists, and their unwillingness to fight was due more to their military weakness. He said that there were 7.000 refugees from Croatia living in Bosanski Novi, and according to Mr. Kirudja, seemed to inadvertently admit that the evacuation of "disloyal" Muslims would have the consequence, intended or not, of making room for Serbs who had been displaced from elsewhere. Mr. Kirudja had the impression that the evacuation of Muslims would not be the last and that a mass expulsion of non-Serbs -- non-Serb populations from Serbian-controlled territory in Bosnia could be expected. At the end of the meeting, Mr. Kirudja informed the Serb delegation that it was absolutely unthinkable that the United Nations would ever be recruited in the manner proposed to make refugees out of people still living in their own homes. Mayor Pasic noted that Mr. Kirudja's attitude was "uncooperative," and asked him for the names of his superiors. On the 1st of June, the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Kupresanin, called Paolo Raffone, a civil affairs member of Mr. Kirudja's staff, and said that the mayors of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most, and Banja Luka had information to the effect that the Muslim population did not trust the Serbian authorities and that 15.000 persons had already left their usual place of residence and started moving toward Dvor and that another 15.000 could follow shortly and that UNPROFOR and the Western countries should find a way to protect the Muslim civilian population. On the 9th of June, Mr. Kirudja received a report from UNHCR containing the summaries of the interviews of two men who had escaped from Bosanski Novi, in which they detailed the -- an attack by the local Serbs. Mr. Kirudja reported up his chain of command about the events he was seeing in Bosnia. For example, on the 16th of June, in a report entitled "Humanitarian Disaster in the Making in Bihac and Along the Bosnian Border," he expressed his fear that "Behind the border, the mountains and the forests, unspeakable atrocities may be unfolding." On the 20th of June, Jens Brosted, the UNHCR protection officer, wrote to the Bosanski Novi Mayor Pasic, reminding him that "The forced mass transfer of population on purely ethnic or racial basis has been declared a crime against humanity in international law." This written admonition reinforced a message that had been orally conveyed repeatedly to him and to his colleagues. On the 22nd of June, another group of persons was spotted on the football stadium in Bosanski Novi. This group signalled the Danish UNPROFOR patrol with white flags and had signalled SOS. On the 4th of July, 1992, Mr. Kirudja sent a report to his superiors, informing them that he believed that the football field detainees were "only the tip of the iceberg involving the concerted action of local Serbian authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina trying to establish a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina free of Muslims." In his lengthy letter, he identified concentration camps -- "concentration camps" at the following locations: "Keraterm, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Manjaca," and he described the treatment of Muslims and other minorities in those camps as "reportedly atrocious, with regular beatings, deprivation of food, water, poor shelter, et cetera." On the 20th of July, the Croatian Prime Minister, Franjo Greguric, reluctantly agreed to permit 4.000 Muslim residents of Bosanski Novi to enter Croatia, and Mr. Kirudja, who remained opposed to the transfer of these people from Bosnia, viewing this as complicity in ethnic cleansing that was likely to recur, assisted UNHCR and UNPROFOR in the movement of these people. The transit through -- this transit of people through Sector North took place. Mr. Kirudja believes that instead of 4.000 people being "evacuated," the number of persons moved exceeded 9.000. The process took an entire day. Prior to the 8th of August, the United Nations civil police in Dvor estimated that another 28.000 persons wished to transit through Sector North. The Serbian authorities claim that the UN had to assist in the evacuation "or the Muslims will suffer." Rather than submit to what UNHCR considered blackmail, the UNHCR declared that it intended to delivery relief supplies directly to the people in question and arrangements were made for 270 tonnes of humanitarian aid to be delivered to Banja Luka. On the 12th of August, a coordination meeting in at Tapusko attended by UNHCR, ICRC, ECMM, UN CIVPOL, the UNMOs, DanBat, and UNHCR's field representative from Sector North concluded that the problem of 28.000 potential refugees was not really a humanitarian problem but rather a political problem related directly to the policy of ethnic cleansing. It was agreed that the solution to the problem could not be found solely by the humanitarian agencies at UNHCR and ICRC and by UNPROFOR. Another meeting was held with the local Serb authorities from Dvor and Bosnia-Herzegovina present, and the UNHCR representative outlined the official response towards any potential refugees. Sobered by the UN Security Council's threats to use force to deliver humanitarian aid, the pressures to organise a convoy to evacuate the potential 28.000 refugees seemed to be dropped. However, the Bosnian Serbs came back, asking for another 5.000 non-Serbs to be evacuated from the area. The individuals making this request included Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, the mayor of Dvor, a representative of the SDS in Bosanska Kostajnica, a representative -- an SDS representative from Kostajnica, and Murid Saflic, a representative of Muslims from Bosanska Kostajnica. The members of the delegation advocated the movement of the 5.000 people. Mayor Pasic said, among other things, that they - referring to the Muslims - realised that "it is impossible to live side by side with the Serbs." And that the Muslims were not "willing to accept their obligations". He went on to say that if the Serbian side is not respected, there could be massive deaths on both sides. Mr. Kirudja and representatives of UNHCR, UN CIVPOL, DanBat refused to acquiesce to another evacuation and the Serbs requested another meeting on the 19th of August. On the 19th of August, a delegation of Serbs and Muslims from Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, and Prijedor arrived at the headquarters in Sector North. The Serb delegation included the SDS president of Sanski Most, Vlado Vrkes, the chief of police from Sanski Most, representatives from Prijedor, and two Bosnian Muslims who represented Muslims and Croats willing to leave Sanski Most and Bosanska Krupa. Mr. Kirudja and two field representatives from UNHCR were present. The Serb Muslim delegation intended to convince the UN to change its policy against mass evacuations and to assist in the organisation of another convoy through Sector North that would serve to evacuate up to 11.000 Muslim "applicants." Mr. Kirudja was given a printed list detailing 7.782 names of persons "ready" to leave voluntarily. Mr. Vrkes, the SDS president of Sanski Most, informed Mr. Kirudja and the UNHCR representatives that the Muslims had been offered a declaration for their signature, stating that the signatories were leaving the area voluntarily, that they had no wish to come back to the area, and that they were leaving their property to the authorities in the respective areas from which they were leaving. The UNHCR representatives rejected the request, stating specifically that UNHCR would not assist with the removal of people but that it would assist people in the location of their present residences and homes. The meeting was concluded. Thereafter, no further requests were made to Mr. Kirudja to have Muslims transit through Sector North. However, well into September, a stream of individuals from Bosnia seeking refuge arrived daily in Dvor in Sector North. UN CIVPOL estimated that between 30 and 50 persons crossed the border into Dvor every day. Your Honour, that concludes the summary of the written evidence submitted in Prosecutor's Exhibit 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I first ask you one question, but I noticed that you -- the summary contains a line about Muslim spokesmen to be identified, the names are mentioned, and one of them is Mr. Bajraktarovic, and it then reads "local SDS leader."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I find that on my -- I'll read it to you as it appears in the transcript. "He informed Mr. Kirudja that two Muslim spokespersons from Bosanski Novi had been identified, a gentleman by the name of S. Bajraktarovic, a local SDS leader, and Fikret," and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing that to my attention. That's clearly an error. That should be SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should be SDA. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had noticed that, but thank you for that correction. We were concerned about that. My only other comment was there was a paragraph, I don't know whether it was just inadvertent to go over that, on page 3 there's a paragraph that starts "On the 6th of May..." Mr. Harmon didn't read that out. He may have simply jumped over it as is easily done. While I'm mentioning it, could I just say that I believe it would be helpful with these 89(F) summaries if acronyms such as DANCON were given a very brief explanation, because otherwise they are a bit mysterious for the very purpose for which these summaries are prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to ask the witness to clarify that. I'm summarising what's literally in the statement and the statement does not have those clarifications in it. That would be augmenting his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The point resolved then, Your Honour, yes. I don't need to pursue that but as long as it's resolved one way or another, no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I may read the paragraph that was omitted that was brought to my attention, I would do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart for bringing that to my attention. The paragraph that was omitted reads as follows: "On the 6th of May, DANCON informed Mr. Kirudja that 350 displaced persons had been gathered on a football field in Bosanski Novi. That they were seen loaded on buses and headed toward an unknown destination in Bosnia. This was the first time that a collection of a large number of people had been detected by DANCON's reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Kirudja, you might wonder why statements are read instead of hearing your testimony. That's done for efficiency reasons, but since we can admit written statements for the public character of this trial, we'd like the public to know what is in that statement, and this does not replace your testimony, but it's just to go through some parts a bit more quickly. You'll certainly get questions about your statement or whatever other subject both by the Prosecution and by the Defence, but not until after the break. We will have a break until a quarter to 1.00, Mr. Harmon, because we had an early first break, so in view of tapes, assistance of interpreters and technicians, we will have to have the second break early as well. So we will adjourn until a quarter to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, Mr. Stewart raised the issue of acronyms, and as you will see and as the Court will see, the exhibits that I propose to tender of awash in a sea of acronyms, so let me just go through these acronyms, and I would like you to confirm what these acronyms mean. UNPA is a United Nations Protected Area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: UNPROFOR stands for United Nations Protection Force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: DANCON or DanBat stands for the Danish Battalion, the military force -- military unit that was assigned in Sector North; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A little amplification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The military forces deployed there came in battalion level, and when we're referring to the entire battalion, then it will be DanBat. Each battalion is made up of military companies. If we're referring to a specific company deployed in a certain location, then it's called DANCON. In that case it will have a prefix like DANCON C, or DANCON company C or company A, that's what it would mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja, for that clarification. UN CIVPOL stands for United Nations Civilian Police?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: ECMM stands for the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: UNMO stands for United Nations Military Observer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, a little amplification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier battalions are formed military fighting forces. Along with those military forces we had teams of military observers deployed separately and parallel with those battalions. So when we are referring -- and they had a separate command structure. So when we're referring to UNMOs, we are referring to those military observers and whatever command system they come under.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. UNHCR stands for United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: ICRC stands for the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think I have hit all the acronyms. We may come across some more in these exhibits and I will ask you about them when we come across them. Thank you. Now, Mr. Kirudja, since you were based in Sector North, why don't we start with a brief explanation by you to the Trial Chamber in respect of the situation in Croatia. Can you tell us what happened in Croatia that led to the creation of the UNPAs, the United Nations Protective Areas?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: United Nations had, of course, in the regular business at its headquarters following that there had been conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and by the end of 1992, the late Secretary of State Cyrus Vance had attempted to deal with that conflict in the former Yugoslavia and had come to a sort of cease-fire, an interim agreement which identified where those areas of conflict were in Croatia and had an agreement that was signed by representatives of the government in Belgrade and in Zagreb, and the representatives in the former -- in Croatia, of those parties that had been engaged in that conflict that were invariably referred to as Croatian Serbs or local Serbs. That agreement became known as the Vance Plan and was codified in a Security Council Resolution which led to the mission United Nations Protection Force being deployed in Croatia in the specific regions that Cyrus Vance had indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me have the next exhibit, a map, shown to you. I take it the exhibit number will be 121. Is that correct? Mr. Kirudja you have before you Prosecutor Exhibit 121. This depicts four separate UN zones or UNPAs. Can you just orient us through this map very quickly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I have a map in front of me here with the title "Map 1," and it shows the Republic of Croatia, and in blue boundaries it depicts where the areas of conflict were and in respect of which the assets of UNPROFOR were to be deployed. You will see on the easternmost part of that map where in red you see Belgium, Luxembourg, and Russia in red, referring to the battalions that were deployed in that area. That area bounded by the blue line became known as Sector East. To the left and west, where you see the caption UN Western Zone, you see in red Argentina, Canada, Jordan, and Nepal, referring to the battalions that were deployed in that area and which in UNPROFOR became known as Sector West. Go to the bottom and the left, where it says UN southern zone, you see Kenya, France, and Czech, referring to the deployment of the battalions from those countries, and it was known as Sector South. And last, you will see UN northern zone, and you see that in red Poland, Denmark, and Nigeria within the area bounded in blue, and somewhere below that, also in red, France but not necessarily in the UNPA area. I will get to that later. But that is Sector North, and that is where I was deployed as the civilian affairs coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next exhibit, Mr. Kirudja. And I take it this next exhibit is a map which bears the number 122. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I have a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, since I have seen this map before, this map depicts, while it says Sector North at the bottom, this depicts not only Sector North but a part of Sector South; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, looking at this map, where the boundary between Sector North and Sector South is located?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There is an area in blue that you can see, and a little below that, if you go to the western middle part of this map where you see the acronym "POL," Poland, and if you go down there, there is a little line there that shows where Poland deployment is, and you could go all the way just north of Titova Korenica. That is where sector north ended. The entire Plitvice Park that you can see there was part of Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the boundary line between Sector North and Sector South?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, the rest of the blue area in the north, of course, is Sector North in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while we're focusing on this map, Mr. Kirudja, I would like you to explain to the Court what became known as pink zones.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This map that you have in front of you, you see in the legend -- let me begin on the legend. The blue line with intermittent dots that says international border, that blue line you can see effectively separates Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia as an international border, and it shows the southernmost edges of United Nations deployment. And you can see it is running all the way to Draksinoc [phoen] on the left-most area. You will then see, guided by the legend on the map, something called "confrontation line," that red thick line that runs above, sometimes below, the blue areas that are Sector North. That is the line depicting, when we arrived, where the Serb forces were still confronting Croatian forces in their foxholes by April when we arrived. That is shown as "confrontation line." Now, what happened was, our mandate was to deploy, in accordance with Vance Plan, that had named earlier, before the UN was deployed, opstina by opstina, meaning municipality by municipality, where the UN would be deployed. So when we arrived, we were easily apprised of a problem in the interpretation of where our boundaries of deployment were going to be, the difference being between the Croatian government side and the Croatian Serbs. I will start with the Croatian government side. They had maps showing we were to be deployed up to the edge of whatever opstina was named by Cyrus Vance, and if you traced the edge of that opstina, that's where you should be deployed according to the Croatian side. And you can see the blue line. That's that. The blue line actually is the edge of each opstina that comprised Sector North. On the left-most, the opstina of Slunj, followed by the opstina of Vojnice, followed by the opstina of Vrgin Most, followed by the opstina of Petrinje, Dvor, and ending with Kostajnica. That would be the edge of where we should be deployed, according to the Croatian side, with a little modification. I won't complicate the explanation beyond that. Not so according to the Serb side. The Serb side had a confrontation -- maps showing where they had taken this war and where they had stopped and where their troops were deployed up to the confrontation line. That is where the Serbs wanted us to be deployed up to that edge. The differences, as you can see, where they are in pink it is where a new opstina, not named in Vance Plan, was involved, and it was behind the confrontation line of the Serbs. And where an opstina named by Cyrus Vance, and the Serbs had not taken their confrontation line up to the edge of that opstina, it will still remain in blue. As you will see on top. But this became such a big problem that these areas which are in pink became a subject of the Security Council Resolution 802 telling us what, in addition to the Vance Plan, our responsibilities were in those zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Now, if the next exhibit could be shown to Mr. Kirudja. This also is a map, Mr. Kirudja, and this will be exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 123. Now, Mr. Kirudja, this is a document you prepared at my request. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this, as we can see above the legend on the top, it says approximately -- "approximate sector boundary," and your signature appears underneath that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This does not purport to be as accurate as a surveyor's map but generally the approximate boundary lines of Sector North; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the purpose of this map, Mr. Kirudja, is to show the municipalities in Bosnia that will be the subject of our discussion throughout your testimony, and I have, for the Court, on the monitor an enlarged version of the area that I'm going to be referring to. But this depicts, does it not, Mr. Kirudja, accurately the location of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanska Dubica, Banja Luka, and other municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, the municipalities bordering on the sector to which we were located and beyond are named in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we're going to be hearing and seeing in documents reference to the Bihac pocket. Can you identify for the Judges the area known as the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Actually, this map is not as good as the one you took away for that purpose. If I may indulge you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: If you can return the map you just gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we get that, I'll withdraw the question and I'll come back to that question because --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It is shown there in total, the pocket and the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will come back to that in just a moment then. The -- actually -- actually, I'll take that back. Why don't we show the previous exhibit to Mr. Kirudja. Referring once again to Prosecutor's Exhibit 122, Mr. Kirudja, can you identify for us the location of the Bihac pocket and tell the Judges what the Bihac pocket was.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have both maps in front of me, and I hope you have both of them in front of you, but I will start with the one I had just been handed over right now. You see yellow. The west part of Bosnia and Herzegovina in yellow. You will see two or three towns inside that yellow. Bihac, see that one? Cazin, and Velika Kladusa, and you see bounded by what is also a boundary of confrontation line by the military, whoever made this map, has bounded. That is the area in our document, and my language we often refer to as the Bihac pocket ourselves, or when the Serbians are speaking to us, they end up referring to it two ways; Cazinska Krajina, or -- yes, you hear that being referred to as Cazinska Krajina. But it is made up by three municipalities; Bihac, which is also a name of the town, the main town. The municipality too is also known as Bihac. Then there is the municipality of Cazin, which is also the town, the name of the town. And then the municipality of Velika Kladusa, which is also the name of a town. On the left-hand part of that, where you see no name, is actually municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we go to Prosecutor's Exhibit 123, I think those municipalities that you identified, Mr. Kirudja, that form the Bihac pocket can clearly be seen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. If we could have the next exhibit, Mr. Kirudja. This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you just one question for my better understanding. If I look at the two maps, P122 and P123, I see that the confrontation lines as depicted, that Bihac, the city of Bihac is in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, we also see on map 123 that the opstina of Bihac is far greater.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're referring to the Bihac pocket, are you referring to the area surrounded by the confrontation lines, that means excluding quite a part of the opstina of Bihac but including the city of Bihac or would it cover the whole opstina of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less the earlier interpretation. It is important to remember, Your Honour, that Bihac was one of the protected safe zones by separate United Nations Security Council, but that came much, much later. So what you see in the boundary there would be more in reference to where that safe area was. When we are talking about the pocket ourselves, we talked about, obviously, most of it, almost all of it, whatever the event led us to. So we were not really too bound by the edges of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Since there's just a short break in Mr. Harmon's questions, we noticed that the three maps that the witness has been looking at so far and the Trial Chamber has seen all have different dates, and although I think it was implicit in one of the answers the witness gave, it might be a help if the witness were possibly asked to give some specific confirmation as to the relevant dates for his evidence so that there isn't any question of any discrepancy as far as dates are concerned, because if there is, it would be better to know that now rather than leave it to be cleared up later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, could you invite the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with these exhibits -- these exhibits bear reference, for example, Prosecutor's Exhibit 121 has at the top a date, "early 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, does this map accurately show the location of the UNPAs in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This is the first map that we started with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Which I don't have here, but I don't need to, I can respond to the question. The question is important, because these maps are taken from the archives of the UN, and as a time line as these events changed when we started in 1992, specifically to the question you raise, would they be accurate representations as of 1992 when we began. It wouldn't be. Because when we started out, Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was zero conflict, there was no presence whatsoever of the UN. As time line developed, they updated the maps, and you will see in that map -- for example in Bihac pocket, you will see -- that's what I said earlier, that is France, battalion from France shown in that map. Even if I don't have it, you should see France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no France in April. There was no one there in April. I mentioned to you earlier when this area became a target of the Security Council much later as a safe area because of the events which will unfold as the evidence comes up, there was a presence of the UN in those areas inside Bosnia. So there is truly a time line to be borne in mind as you look at these maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the purpose of these maps is just to show general locations and accurate locations in relation to Bosnia. I don't want to dwell and it is not in issue where the boundaries are in Croatia. It's just for purposes of orienting us geographically for purposes of understanding Mr. Kirudja's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you permit, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be glad to have that confirmed. I'm sorry. We would be glad to have that confirmed, but I must say that the detail then in which we've gone into these matters in the last 15 minutes or so, it raises the question whether that was of any great value.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I want to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was responding to Mr. Harmon primarily, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep it orderly. I blame myself for interfering in examination in chief. Mr. Harmon, I would like the witness to clarify the issue and then we go again in the normal orders. Please tell us what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, at the time, those maps are accurate with regard to the deployment of UN troops in the UNPA. So that the map is accurate when it shows you the deployment of DanBat, PolBat, and all those units in the UNPA, the map is accurate regardless of the future development of the events. My comment was only limited to any deployment of battalions you see across the international border into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next exhibit, please, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 124. Mr. Kirudja, you have that before you. Again, Mr. Kirudja, this exhibit is a map prepared by you showing the approximate location, boundary lines of Sector North. It bears your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And again bearing in mind the comment from the learned counsel, the date of this map and boundaries were drawn in connection with another testimony in a different trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But the purpose of this map really, Mr. Kirudja, is to identify some cities that are located in Sector North. Tapusko, that was the location of your headquarters in Sector North; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to be hearing about the city of Dvor, which is also marked on the boundary line between Bosanski Novi and Dvor; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That was the location, was it not, of the Danish battalion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Again, amplification. The battalion headquarters, the Danish battalion headquarters was in Kostajnica. The company, Company C, their headquarters was in Dvor and their other headquarters of different companies that are not shown here but if they are mentioned in the text we could clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, also marked in pink, I believe, are locations that we'll be hearing about in your testimony and in the exhibits that are located in Bosnia; Bosanski Novi, Blagaj, Japra, Suhaca, Donji Agici, and Gornji Agici; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Kirudja, which ethnic group controlled Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: On arrival, when we deployed in this sector, within those approximate boundaries, that area was under the control of what I mentioned as Croatian Serbs as -- or local Serbs, depending on the appellation that was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on the Vance Plan. If you could very quickly summarise for us, what was the Vance Plan and what were its priorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Vance Plan basically gave us our mandate and our guidelines of what it is we had to accomplish while we were deployed there. For simplicity, I can distil that into three sequentially interlinked priorities. The first priority was this area had already military units facing each other. Our priority was to demilitarise and demobilise those units that were already facing each other when we arrived and caused them to agree to give up all the weaponry they had militarily deployed in that area, and in accordance to the Vance, they had agreed to place those weaponry in the hands of the United Nations forces, those -- and that they had agreed there would be what was known as the double key. They would have a key to those weapons, and we would have another key, like in a combination lock in a bank where two people are required to go and recover the contents. That's priority number one. Priority number two, because there is no authority or, rather, because the Croatian government authority was not effective in that area, Vance Plan and the UN Security Council recognised someone had to have both authority and the responsibility for day-to-day order that would be kept in there. According to the Vance Plan, we had recognised only the municipal structures that existed prior to the conflict, meaning the mayor and the local police of each opstina was a recognised authority. Their responsibility was law and order. We didn't have that responsibility. Very important. That was their responsibility. Ours was to monitor how they executed that responsibility for law and order. They were allowed to keep the police forces they had, only on condition that those police forces had light side-weapons. We deployed our own civilian police to monitor how they went about exercising that responsibility for law and order. That's priority number two. Priority number three, we had as a mandate, as a mission, to ensure that the conditions would improve such that all those people who had been displaced or run away from there as refugees would have the ability to return there voluntarily, and that was the component of civil affairs component that would look into the humanitarian and the local infrastructure that would be improved such that the people would want to come back by themselves. Footnote: You notice with those three responsibilities I didn't mention any political responsibility to solve the basic problem that led to the conflict. This mission, when it started, didn't have that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at the time you were in Sector North, where was -- was there a headquarters component to your organisation that was located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct. And it ties to the last remark I made, that the mission didn't have the mandate to sort the basic problem that led to the fighting in the first place, but the UN assumed that this fighting was only limited to Croatia, and there were no signs of any problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in their estimation at that time, the UN headquarters decided, for neutrality or impartiality's sake, the headquarters -- the UNPROFOR headquarters would be deployed in Sarajevo rather than anywhere either in Belgrade or in Zagreb where the signatories enabling this mission were validated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I would like to focus on your staff in Sector North. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about your staff, the numbers of people working for you and with you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I will give you an overview of how all the assets that we had worked with each other. We had the military side of our assets. That was as we discussed earlier; three battalions, each battalion was with three companies deployed inside that area that you have in front of you. Each battalion had its headquarters, and we had our headquarters in Tapusko, coordinating all those areas. On the other hand, we had civil police, commanded by a chief of police who was in Tapusko. We had various units often co-located with the military but separate and distinct from the military companies, known as police CIVPOL units. We had military observers, as I mentioned earlier, deployed on the edges of this map, often across in the confrontation line in places like Karlovac, Zagreb, Sisak, and across the international boundary in Velika Kladusa, in Bihac. We had military units and their deployment around that. We had also civil affairs officers, and we had a full contingent that were both civil and political affairs that were deployed accordingly. In other words, there was a totality of information and flow arriving at my headquarters from all these assets. I mention this so you get an understanding of what you have from me, where it comes from. From all these resources as they are deployed in that manner, all of them generating as a requirement a flow of information up each command line; the military command line, the military observers' command line, the civil police command line, the civil affairs, and all of them coming into our situation room in Tapusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, also operating in Sector North, I believe, were representatives of ICRC, ECMM, and UNHCR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct. And those were also deployed in their own command -- deployment areas but coordinating very much with us. As a matter of fact, the UNHCR was located in our headquarters. The ICRC, because of its mandate, obviously, would not be co-located with us, but they were also co-located inside the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And those representatives from those NGOs were also a source of information for you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Pretty much so. And very often they would be not only the source but we would be invited or they would invite us to certain meetings when we thought their presence was necessary, which was very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the preparation of reports. Can you describe about -- can you give us some help about the preparation of reports, how often they were prepared, why they were prepared, and where they went.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: As you can understand in a large organisation like the United Nations, there are reporting requirements and designated channels of information. Each of these assets were required to report up their chain of command daily, and that situation room I described was the nerve centre of reports that would be coming from these various units, and I had, obviously, full access to that flow of information coming in that situation room along those channels, as I mentioned. On top of that, I had, as the senior-most civilian, dealings with non-official channels. When people wanted to discuss or even complain about the UN, I was the address where they came. So there were other non-official interactions that actually came into that area and addressed to the civil affairs coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive information from local Serbs, local Croats, Serbs, Croats, Muslims from Bosnia as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Indeed. Because this was a country prior to the fighting that was seamlessly connected, very early that area that we talked about called Bihac was a nerve centre of life, not just in Bihac but in the surrounding area, that is the confrontation line. The largest hospital was in Bihac. A huge airport was in Bihac. Immediately there was a confrontation line, the people were cut off. And there is only one or two arteries of roads which had to pass through there. So if they wanted to go to Zagreb, on the left-hand corner there is one artery. If they wanted to go to Sisak, on the other. And all of that passed through this Serb-controlled area. If anyone who came in there who was not Serb, they couldn't do that without our help. So almost within the month, April, May we were there, we were seized with requests, can we transit, can we -- can you help us this way or that way across the border from Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also receive information from refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Information?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: As the refugees came through requesting help to transition through that -- through that sector, we would ask, "What are you running away from? What is the problem?" And slowly by slowly as they came, we got to hear their stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you, in your reports, attempt to analyse the situation or give information about the political situation in your theatre, about the military situation, and about social developments?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We're duty-bound to do that, to keep our superiors aware of the reality that they had assumed in the mission and how that reality was playing out. Example: Assuming peace across the border from Bosnia was an assumption which was rapidly proving to be untenable. So part of our reporting is not just to report that a hundred -- the first time ten people came looking for assistance to cross, the reasons why they were looking for that assistance had to be part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And those people who were debriefed as they were coming across the border, they were debriefed by representatives from the UNHCR, by representatives from ICRC, by the civilian police, by UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Indeed. They were telling their stories at the point as -- depending on how comfortable they felt with whoever they are looking at. In the first place, they may not have been comfortable and were too frightened to talk. So depending on who it is they had met, they would tell their story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a convenient place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I asked Mr. Harmon to ask Mr. Tieger to come for the last ten minutes -- there are only five remaining minutes -- because the Chamber would like to inform the parties about an issue which is irrelevant for this witness. So, Mr. Kirudja, you're excused for the day, but we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom, and I want to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given today or the testimony still to be given in the days to come. So please, would you keep that in your mind, and then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kirudja out the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure Mr. Tieger is outside the courtroom. With the Court's permission, could I use this phone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is on his way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He is on his way. Then we will ... Mr. Tieger, I asked you to come to the courtroom because I'd like to inform the parties, and there's hardly any time left, but perhaps even get a very brief response or at least give an opportunity to give any comment in 30 seconds. The Chamber has still to decide on the issue of 92 bis in respect of the testimony of Mr. Babic, which we expect next week. It took us quite some time to get a good oversight over the material, because although you made the selection, it is a selection of 1.100 pages out of 1.250. So therefore the Chamber is a bit concerned that 92 bis might become counter-productive to its own aims, and therefore 1.100 pages, 87 exhibits of which the Chamber, and of course it took us some time to have at least a global look at it even if we didn't analyse it every single line. We also have some concerns about the level of relevance. I'm not saying that it's irrelevant, and everything is related to everything, but the level of relevance of the whole of the testimony, even the selected pages, is not always that clear and we see quite a different level of relevance on some parts as well. Another issue is that, as you know, this Chamber is very much concerned about the public character of this trial, and how to handle 1.100 pages of 92 bis by giving summaries is not something that at least is resolved by just putting it on the Chamber's table. Therefore, the Chamber has provisionally made up its mind on how to deal with the matter, and although the Defence has not objected the admission of all of the 1.100 pages and the 87 exhibits, the Chamber would like to deal with it in a different way. But before giving a final decision, I think -- of course we have to write that down and to give a proper reasoning -- first of all I would like to confront you with it, what I'm doing at this very moment, and at the same time give you an opportunity, we have not many days left, at least already to start thinking about how to solve it. On from this very moment. The Chamber is inclined to solve the matter in the following way: We will not admit 1.100 pages of transcript. We will not admit 87 exhibits, but we'll not -- we're not saying we will not admit them, but we want this material to fit into the viva voce testimony. Just to give you an example of what we have in mind: For example, if the witness comes at a certain moment during his viva voce testimony, he comes to a -- well, let's say he comes to the arrest of Mr. Martic or if he comes to any disagreement on what position in a political meeting to take, that you could then switch from your viva voce testimony. Say, for example, if you touch upon that point, you say, well, Mr. Martic was arrested or was not arrested and then you could ask the witness, Did you testify about the arrest of Mr. Martic in the Milosevic case? And then introduce the relevant portion but then relate it linked to the viva voce testimony of that moment to introduce the relevant portion by way of 92 bis. That means that you'd say you testified, you then address the Chamber and say we find this on pages so-and-so and so in the transcript, and you give, for example, a summary of three or four lines on what this testimony was at that time so that we get linked every portion of transcript to the evidence we receive at that moment. That would require you to make another selection, as a matter of fact, and not 1.100 pages out of 1.250 but to fit that in the line of your questioning. The Chamber would then very much like you to already indicate to the Defence this and this and this will be the portions we'll use in support, because that's then how it will be used, in support of the viva voce evidence, avoiding that we have to go into every detail if we touch upon a certain subject if these details are not of that major importance so that the Defence is able to prepare on it. And I'm aware that it takes some additional effort to do this. And of course we will then admit that portion of the transcript in evidence, and therefore you should keep carefully in mind that of course it should meet the requirements of 92 bis (D). That means it should not deal with the acts and the conduct of the accused. A similar approach would then be for the -- for the exhibits. So the Chamber expects, as a matter of fact, looking at the level of relevance and the level of detail sometimes, and also the focus on Mr. Milosevic very often or on Croatia in the Milosevic testimony, we would then expect that the final number of pages could be a smaller part of what you had in mind when you introduced the 1.100 pages. Well, we can -- the Chamber was thinking about not more than 200 in bits and pieces well located into the viva voce testimony. That's what we have in mind. We have not much time left. First of all, you should not be confronted with it too late, but it really took us some time to see how we could resolve this matter and how we could avoid that 92 bis instead of adding to the efficiency would finally augment enormously to the material that would otherwise never have been introduced in evidence. This is what we are inclined to decide. This is what we made up our mind and to now professionally will very quickly deliver a decision, but I'd like to give you if it were only half of one minute to just -- to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, thank you for the opportunity to address the Court on this issue. I want to separate the prospect of the solution the Court has crafted as a general response and helpful refinement of the 92 bis process from my concerns about the application of this solution in this case. My main concern is that it does come late in the day. I have attempted to craft an examination in court that meets the concerns the Court addressed, including the public nature of the trial and the specification or identification of relevance. This -- it would be a considerable exercise to re-craft it at this point, although the preparations were based on the absence of an objection and the appearance that it was proceeding in that fashion. I can also say that I think at this point, after the efforts that have been undertaken by all parties, including the legal officers and the Court, it would now add more time to the process. I hope to move -- I'd hoped to take advantage of the fact that we appeared to have arrived at a stage of general agreement about that material and focus in court on a summary that would identify the relevance and move us through very quickly and then a primary focus on that information which is more appropriate for viva voce testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the response from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we would -- we'd prefer not to have to give a response immediately. We see -- except to say that we do see a very great deal of force and common sense, if I may respectfully say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is grateful --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- for what the Chamber is suggesting. When we don't we very politely, I hope, Your Honour, when we don't see those elements we usually do make our view plain as well, I hope politely and respectfully to the Trial Chamber. Though in this particular case we genuinely do. Your Honour if I were to say more, I think I would get into the broader issues of how effectively and efficiently the parties could resolve exactly this sort of issue if we had the opportunity of doing it. And one of the reasons why we didn't put any specific objections and to raise any specific matters in relation to Mr. Babic's testimony is frankly we simply didn't have the time to do it, and we just took a robust decision that we just had to put that on one side and just let others sort it out. It's not a satisfactory way of proceeding, Your Honour. You know our views on that. We would be grateful for the opportunity of -- well, first of all, I'd like to discuss it with my team as well. May we give some thoughts on this in the morning, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you could do that. May I suggest, Mr. Tieger, having listened to you, would -- would a delay of the decision, and then I'm mainly focusing on the transcripts more than on the introduction of the -- of the statement of Mr. Babic under 89(F), the new statement, the statement focusing more on the Krajisnik case rather than on the Milosevic case. As far as the transcripts are concerned, would it be a solution that at the end of the testimony, where sometimes perhaps reference is made to parts of the transcript, which has happened a couple of times, yesterday and today as well, that we say well, having heard the testimony and having seen where we touched upon certain subjects of the earlier testimony, that we then define what pages are really of importance to have admitted into evidence. Because otherwise, we get a lot of books where there's no direct relation any more with what happened in the courtroom. The link between the testimony and the 92 bis, especially here where Mr. Babic appears to testify. It would be different if it is a witness of course who testified on a limited subject, but this is a huge number of subjects which, just by reading, not always the relevance the Prosecution sees in it is always clear enough and which would make it more difficult to -- for the parties to digest and also for the Chamber to digest the material and to evaluate it in a proper way. Would perhaps -- but perhaps you could think that over as well, that we then limit the number or identify the specific relevant portions of the testimony during the testimony of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I suggest a compromise solution which I hope satisfies our mutual concerns as we've expressed them today, and perhaps that could be that that decision could be made after -- after the testimony and also on the basis of the summary of the 92 bis testimony that the Court hears, which has been prepared. And that way if the -- there is material that falls outside the ambit of both the testimony and the summary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have summarised all the 1.100 pages with all the subjects as we find them on the subject index?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would say it's fair to say I took the submitted material and provided what I hoped would be the most useful summary to the Court. I suspect that if the Court were to draw some kind of conceptual boundaries around that summary you would find material that's included in the submitted material that doesn't fall within there, and that might be a way of refining or reducing the scope of the actual submitted material, and of course I would be happy to work with the Court officers in identifying where those areas can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would not mind if you would take a bit more time then for the examination-in-chief. I mean, we do understand that it might take you a bit more time. I think you suggested on the basis of the 1.100 pages and the 87 exhibits that you would need another six hours. If -- if would you take, well, let's say, eight or perhaps even nine or ten and if the Defence would take another, well, 60 per cent of that time, approximately, but perhaps here we should be a bit more balanced and not stick that much to the 60 per cent rule as to -- it's not really a rule but -- but I would say a mutual expectation at this moment, then it would not -- we could take a bit more time to compensate a bit for the reduction or at least the more strict selection of material that would be then finally submitted and admitted into evidence. We could leave the decision until after we heard the testimony, although then of course whatever has been touched upon during the viva voce testimony, it should be clear that of course it should become part of the evidence. So we have to take decisions then. But whatever has not been touched upon but is nevertheless in these transcripts, we could delay a decision perhaps on that. Let's give it some thought. I express the concern of the Chamber. We will have to come with a decision anyhow soon, but the Chamber thought it wise just to inform you about it. The Chamber, on the other hand, would very much like to finish the testimony of Mr. Babic next week. So -- and I ask the parties to be as efficient as possible in that respect. So when I say the Chamber wouldn't mind if six hours would be eight, the Chamber would mind if it would be ten or 11 or 12, because we might not finish then next week, and that's for various reasons of some report. Although, finally, the Chamber is also aware that sometimes matters develop in such a way that it would be unfair to say we have to stop because we decided we would not take more time, and that's -- I mean, finally, the fairness is the basic -- the basic aspect and nothing else. So when I urge the parties to see whether we can try to deal with it in some four days with some support of written material but also limited, that we'd very much like to finish next week but if it's impossible, then time schedules, finally, are not the decisive element. I took already far too much time from the interpreters. I apologise for that. Mr. Tieger is to be blamed for just five minutes, but I took 15 minutes more, so I'm double to be blamed. The same for technicians. Unless there would be something that really needs to be said at this very moment, I'd like to spend a couple of minutes tomorrow morning again and then we'll decide on the matter. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
